content:
I recently noticed that Apple seems to have abandoned the "Cinematic" mode, and a video test perfectly demonstrates my disappointment with this.

The disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because it's almost at a practically usable level, making it hard to understand why Apple hasn't taken advantage of the massive leap in processing power from the iPhone 13 that first featured it all the way to the latest iPhone. Let me show you…

I've mentioned before that I understand why Apple hasn't prioritized updating this feature, but at the same time I also think Apple should update it to encourage the next generation of videographers and filmmakers—especially teenagers who might not have any other camera equipment to use.

I have a friend who likes to use a smartphone to interview strangers on the street, and remarkably they can always get them to open up and say the most unexpected things. I decided to turn the tables and put them in the interviewee's seat, also shooting with a smartphone, and this time I used the iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to test "Cinematic" mode in a relatively simple scene: there's a person in the foreground, a railing roughly 25 feet behind them, and the O2 Arena on the other side of the river is estimated to be thousands of feet away. In addition, they would be sitting on a tall stool, meaning the amount of movement is quite limited.

The result was…so close, yet so far. The overall impression is good, but there's noticeable halation between CK's legs and the railing, and when he moves his head and blocks one of the O2's pillars, it sometimes loses focus; when he spreads his arms, the river behind him occasionally comes into sharp focus:

To be fair, CK thinks most viewers watching the footage wouldn't actually notice the problems. If they're not filmmakers, or tech enthusiasts familiar with how this feature works, they wouldn't think there's an issue even if they did notice. I think he's absolutely right.

But these flaws really do bother me, and I think even amateur-level cinema enthusiasts would feel the same disappointment—and these people are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the very beginning, my disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because I truly believe that if Apple were to properly leverage the powerful computational capabilities and neural processing performance of current iPhone chips, this feature could be dramatically improved. In fact, I'd expect a truly updated "Cinematic" mode to be able to handle far more complex shooting environments than this.

Do you agree with my view? Do you want to see Apple pay some attention to "Cinematic" mode? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
